fr:frontmatter.fr:title: CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution
fr:frontmatter.fr:meta: @misc{yeCAKECompilerAgentCoDesign2026, title = {{{CAKE}}: {{Compiler-Agent Co-Design}} for {{Frontier Kernel Evolution}}}, author = {Ye, Zihao and Huang, Yingyi and Jin, Hongyi and Hou, Bohan and Shao, Junru and Yu, Zhongming and Chen, Jinqi and Cowan, Meghan and Cao, Shiyi and Xing, Shanli and Chen, Hanfeng and Grover, Vinod and Chen, Tianqi and Ceze, Luis}, year = {2026}, doi = {10.48550/ARXIV.2608.12629}, urldate = {2026-08-15}, publisher = {arXiv}, file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/CAKE Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution - Ye et al..pdf}, keywords = {FOS: Computer and information sciences,Machine Learning (cs.LG)}, copyright = {arXiv.org perpetual, non-exclusive license}, abstract = {Work on GPU kernel agents and work on GPU programming languages have advanced separately, and the gap between them is where expert kernels are lost. Kernel agents treat the compiler as a fixed black box: they improve proposal, mutation, and ranking, but the environment returns only compiler errors, correctness outcomes, and end-to-end timing---signals that never say which program decision caused a synchronization failure, a hardware-contract violation, or a pipeline stall, and that cannot grow when a frontier workload exposes a missing capability. Meanwhile the languages an agent might write are not built for one. Tile-level DSLs hide the warp specialization, barrier choreography, and memory-tier placement that separate expert kernels from merely correct ones; low-level DSLs expose that control but demand a layout calculus that makes agent errors both likely and hard to localize. We present Cake, which codesigns the two. Agents author Cake IR, a typed, hardware-explicit schedule representation that gives fine-grained control without a layout algebra and carries enough information for a verifier and cost model to reason about a program before it is compiled; the harness answers with localized correctness and performance diagnostics and is itself a target of evolution, so recurring failures become new verifier rules, IR primitives, cost-model calibrations, and reusable tactics rather than one-off workarounds. Across matched implementation-hidden Flash-KMeans clean starts on B200 (three runs per representation), the best candidate at an 80-million-token budget reaches a median 1.144\texttimes{} the tuned FlashML baseline with Cake IR, versus 0.928\texttimes{} for direct CUDA/PTX. Beyond the clean-start benchmark, agent-generated Kimi Delta Attention reaches a 2.05\texttimes{} geometric-mean speedup over official FlashKDA and is validated in end-to-end serving. Dispatcher-backed KNN and KMeans families improve performance by 1.42\texttimes --2.12\texttimes{} across more than 400 shapes, and four kernel changes are available as upstream PRs. Cake targets NVIDIA GPUs from Ampere through Blackwell and separates single-shape evolution from the generalization and dispatch stage required for library integration.}, month = {August}, shorttitle = {{{CAKE}}} }

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization
fr:frontmatter.fr:meta: @misc{tschandJAXBenchBenchmarkingAutonomous2026, title = {{{JAXBench}}: {{Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization}}}, author = {Tschand, Arya and Hong, Charles and Walker, Julian and Cai, Nina and Wang, Shangkun and Subramanian, Suvinay and Dev, Sundar and Reddi, Vijay Janapa and Yazdanbakhsh, Amir and Sankaran, Sethu}, year = {2026}, doi = {10.48550/arXiv.2607.20466}, urldate = {2026-08-03}, number = {arXiv:2607.20466}, publisher = {arXiv}, file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/JAXBench Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization - Tschand et al..pdf}, keywords = {Computer Science - Artificial Intelligence}, langid = {english}, archiveprefix = {arXiv}, abstract = {Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel performance optimization by establishing a shared target to hillclimb on, but no equivalent exists for TPUs. We present JAXBench, a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs. JAXBench comprises 50 JAX workloads that are both relevant and provide headroom for optimization. We extract 17 production ML operators from architectures in the public MaxText library such as Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, and AlphaFold2, and translate 33 operators from KernelBench that are validated for correctness and set with new problem sizes that achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight of the 17 production operators ship with hand-optimized Pallas kernels from the public Tokamax library and block-size tuned to establish an expert upper-bound baseline. We evaluate four feedback-driven methods on generating candidate Pallas kernels for JAXBench. Across the full suite with Gemini 3 Flash, we find that target-specific context matters more than model scale on a sparsely-documented DSL like Pallas. Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8\% to 37.3\% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks at a 1.28x geomean speedup. Search structure yields significant gains once correctness is achieved, with Autocomp's beam-search pipeline reaching a 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on the specialized paged and ragged attention operators. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains a challenging task, and we release the JAXBench benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results to support open source contributions.}, primaryclass = {cs.AI}, eprint = {2607.20466}, month = {May}, shorttitle = {{{JAXBench}}} }

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This is the harder part (and requires the most discipline). When working on a task, especially a more open-ended one like research, it is very common that a million other things come up that seem immediately important. All of the sudden, you have a great idea for the research project you haven't worked on in months.

It is crucial to collect and forget about these things until they are scheduled. This is the one thing I did take from Getting Things Done. The system should flow like water. Making this achievable is where the todoist API becomes crucial.

html:ul.html:li: I have a script bound by dwm that pops up vim for me to write down the task and, on save, it sends it to my inbox in todoist.
I have more involved ones that allow me to actually allocate it to the specific work stream / priority if it is immediately obvious.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Another thing that I have found useful to actually achieving this watery flow is the pomodoro technique. This basically lets me gaslight myself into thinking I can go to the other things as soon as the timer ends (which is intentionally always just close enough). By the end, I often no longer have this urge and can continue on the scheduled tasks.
A core component of the TPU architecture responsible for performing matrix multiplication via a weight stationary Systolic array.

html:ul.html:li: 128 \times 128 — 16,384 multiply accumulate units, each multiplying and adding in one cycle. v6e/Trillium widens the array to 256 \times 256, i.e. 65,536.
The native op is one bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, or about 5e13 bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz. A v5e chip has enough MXUs to reach ~2e14.

fr:mainmatter.html:div:
Remark. The side length is fixed in hardware, so every dimension has to be tiled down to it and any axis shorter than it is padded up to it, wasting the FLOPs spent on the padding. The order is
Tiling the matrix to load from HBM to VMEM.
Compiler tiles from VMEM to 128 \times 128 tiles to load into the MXU.

fr:title.text: Why the MXU pads everything to 128

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the MXU pads everything to 128

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the native op of one Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and why does that force padding to 128?

html:div.html:details:
Answer One bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, on a 128 \times 128 systolic array — 256 \times 256 on v6e/Trillium.
The array's side length is fixed in hardware, so any matrix axis shorter than 128 (256 on v6e) is padded up to it, and the FLOPs spent on the padding are simply wasted. With 2–4 MXUs per core, tiling dimensions want to exceed 128 \times the MXU count.
Scale: roughly 5e13 bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz, so about 2e14 per v5e chip. int8 runs ~2\times faster, int4 ~4\times .
